questions.q: What specific gap does the reviewing architect find in Lesson 15's Access-request approval subflow?
options: The subflow approves access requests without checking domain boundaries at all
A null return from the approver-resolution check silently stops the subflow, leaving the requester's ticket unresolved with no error or notification to anyone
The subflow was never tested against any real data
The subflow routes every Access request to the wrong assignment group
questions.explain: The gap is specific: fail-closed behavior is correct, but a null return currently has no visible fallback -- the request just silently stops.

questions.q: Why does the reviewer agree that "failing closed" on a cross-domain manager mismatch was the right original decision?
options: Fail closed is slower than fail open, which is always preferable
Fail closed should be removed entirely in the revision
Reversing it would risk auto-approving an access request across a domain boundary that was never supposed to be crossed
Fail closed was never actually implemented in Lesson 15
questions.explain: The critique isn't about the decision to fail closed -- that's exactly correct -- it's about treating that refusal as a complete answer on its own.

questions.q: What makes this peer-review critique "genuine and specific" rather than a vague compliment or vague worry?
options: It names the exact code path, the exact missing behavior, and the exact person affected, instead of a general "looks good" or unfocused concern
It simply states that the build is impressive without further detail
It avoids referencing any actual code or logic from the build
It focuses only on code style and formatting, not behavior
questions.explain: A real peer review reads the actual logic and names a specific path and its concrete consequence, not a generic reaction.

questions.q: What pattern does the revision reuse from elsewhere in this capstone, rather than inventing something new?
options: The ADR format from Lesson 18's deployment documentation
The domain-routing Script Include's own named, documented fallback behavior for a missing domain mapping
The staged go-live sequencing from Lesson 14's scoping decision
The category compromise model from Lesson 14
questions.explain: Lesson 15's routing script already falls back to a named corporate default queue instead of guessing or silently dropping a request -- the approval subflow gets the same shape of fallback.

questions.q: Why does a safe failure that nobody can see still count as a real problem for this capstone, given Lesson 13's Prairie View interview?
options: Because employees experience a silently unresolved request the same way they'd experience the new system losing their request -- exactly the kind of silent breakage that undercuts the trust Prairie View specifically asked for
Because Prairie View has no Access-category requests at all
Because silent failures are only a cosmetic concern with no real impact on trust
Because the subflow's domain check was itself incorrect
questions.explain: A technically correct fail-closed outcome that's invisible to the requester and their domain still erodes the trust Lesson 13 made a real, explicit requirement.
